questions.question: What's the difference between `Future` and `CompletableFuture`? When would you still use plain `Future`?
questions.title: `Future` vs `CompletableFuture` — Blocking Handle vs Composable Async
questions.direct_answer: **`Future<T>`** (Java 5) is just a **blocking result handle** — you get it back from `ExecutorService.submit()` and call `.get()` to wait for the result. No callbacks, no composition, no exception handling beyond rethrow on `get()`, cannot be completed manually. **`CompletableFuture<T>`** (Java 8) implements `Future<T>` but adds a full **composable async API**: callbacks (`thenApply`), composition (`thenCompose`, `thenCombine`), exception recovery (`exceptionally`, `handle`), manual completion (`.complete(value)`), and executor control (`*Async(executor)`). **Use plain `Future`** only when you're legitimately working with an API that returns it and you really do just want to block on the result (batch jobs, simple `Callable` tasks). **Everywhere else use `CompletableFuture`** — modern HTTP clients, message handling, parallel fan-out. On Java 21+, for purely I/O-bound code, virtual threads with simple blocking calls often replace CompletableFuture chains entirely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows CompletableFuture is a superset (it implements Future) and why that matters; understands the limitations of plain Future that make it unsuitable for non-trivial async code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Future is asynchronous (it isn't — `.get()` blocks). Using plain Future for complex async flows where composition would help
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that CompletableFuture implements Future so it's drop-in; mention that virtual threads on Java 21 often replace CompletableFuture chains for I/O-bound code; highlight the commonPool trap with supplyAsync

sections.title: The Distinction in One Sentence
sections.content:
`Future` is a **result handle**. `CompletableFuture` is a **programmable async pipeline**.

Both represent "a value that may not exist yet." The key difference is what you can do with that representation:

- **`Future`** — you can check `isDone()`, cancel, or **block on `get()`**. That's it. No way to attach a callback. No way to chain with another async op without blocking.
- **`CompletableFuture`** — implements `Future<T>` (so it's a drop-in replacement wherever `Future` is expected) but adds:
  - **Callbacks**: `thenApply`, `thenAccept`, `thenRun`
  - **Composition**: `thenCompose`, `thenCombine`, `applyToEither`
  - **Fan-in**: `CompletableFuture.allOf`, `anyOf`
  - **Exception handling**: `exceptionally`, `handle`, `whenComplete`
  - **Manual completion**: `.complete(value)`, `.completeExceptionally(ex)`
  - **Timeouts** (Java 9+): `orTimeout`, `completeOnTimeout`
  - **Executor control**: `*Async(fn, executor)` variants

The practical implication: any non-trivial async code written with plain `Future` degenerates to a forest of `get()` calls and blocking. `CompletableFuture` lets you write async flows declaratively.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Capability | `Future<T>` | `CompletableFuture<T>` |
|---|---|---|
| **Get result** | `get()` (blocks), `get(timeout)` | `get()`, `join()`, `getNow(default)` |
| **Check status** | `isDone()`, `isCancelled()` | Same + `isCompletedExceptionally()` |
| **Cancel** | `cancel(boolean)` | Same |
| **Attach callback** | ❌ | ✅ `thenApply/Accept/Run` |
| **Chain async op** | ❌ (must block and resubmit) | ✅ `thenCompose` |
| **Combine two futures** | ❌ | ✅ `thenCombine`, `allOf`, `anyOf` |
| **Handle exception** | ❌ (only thrown from `get()`) | ✅ `exceptionally`, `handle` |
| **Manual completion** | ❌ | ✅ `complete(v)`, `completeExceptionally(e)` |
| **Timeout on the future** | ❌ (only on `get()`) | ✅ `orTimeout`, `completeOnTimeout` (Java 9+) |
| **Executor control** | Tied to the submitting executor | ✅ per-stage via `*Async(fn, executor)` |
| **Implements `Future`** | Yes (it is `Future`) | Yes (subtype of `Future`) |
| **Implements `CompletionStage`** | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Typical source** | `ExecutorService.submit()` | `supplyAsync`, `runAsync`, manual, chain |

sections.title: Plain `Future` — Pain at Scale
`CompletableFuture` — Declarative Composition
The `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` Trap
sections.content:
`CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task)` **without an executor argument** runs `task` on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool` — default parallelism = `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1`. That's a tiny pool sized for CPU-bound work.

If `task` is **blocking I/O**, it occupies a commonPool thread for the entire I/O. A few dozen such calls can saturate commonPool, stalling every parallel stream and CompletableFuture in the JVM.

**Always pass an executor for blocking work**:
```java
Executor io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50,
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("io-%d").build());
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.get(url), io);
```

Or on Java 21:
```java
Executor io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
```

This is the single most common production bug in CompletableFuture code.

sections.title: Virtual Threads — The Java 21 Shift
sections.content:
Java 21's virtual threads change when CompletableFuture is the right tool.

**Before Java 21**: for server-side I/O-bound code, CompletableFuture was the main way to get concurrency without thread-pool exhaustion. Every "fetch from 5 services and combine" was a `thenCombine` chain.

**Java 21+**: virtual threads let you write simple blocking code that scales:
```java
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<User> userF = executor.submit(() -> userService.fetch(id));
    Future<List<Order>> ordersF = executor.submit(() -> orderService.fetch(id));
    Future<Prefs> prefsF = executor.submit(() -> prefsService.fetch(id));
    
    return build(userF.get(), ordersF.get(), prefsF.get()); // blocking is fine!
}
```

This uses plain `Future<T>` — blocking on `.get()` on a virtual thread unmounts the carrier, freeing it for other work. The code is simpler than CompletableFuture chains.

**When to still use CompletableFuture on Java 21**:
- Callback-based library integration (you're wrapping a non-blocking API).
- True parallel fan-out with combinators (`allOf(f1,...,f100)`).
- Complex pipelines with exception recovery at multiple stages.

**When plain Future + virtual threads wins on Java 21**:
- Sequential I/O calls in a request handler.
- Two-to-three parallel calls where blocking `.get()` is readable.
- Existing code that's hard to refactor into CompletableFuture style.

sections.title: When Each is Right
sections.content:
**Use plain `Future`**:
- Working with an API that returns `Future` and you truly just want to block.
- Simple single-task submission: `Future<?> f = pool.submit(task); f.get();`
- Java 21 + virtual threads: blocking `.get()` is cheap; `CompletableFuture` composition may be overkill.
- Testing callable tasks where you care only about success/failure and blocking is fine.

**Use `CompletableFuture`**:
- Any non-trivial async flow with composition, timeouts, or exception recovery.
- Wrapping callback-based libraries (create a CompletableFuture and complete it in the callback).
- Fan-out to multiple services with declarative combinators.
- Building async APIs that other code will chain onto.

**Don't use `CompletableFuture`**:
- For back-pressured streaming — use Reactor `Flux` or RxJava `Observable`.
- For pure CPU work — use parallel streams or `ForkJoinPool` directly.
- As the only tool when virtual threads would simplify the code.

**Watch out for**:
- Returning `CompletableFuture` without terminating it (no `exceptionally`/`handle`/`get`) — exceptions are lost silently.
- Using `supplyAsync` without an executor for blocking work — saturates commonPool.
- Mixing plain `Future` and `CompletableFuture` in the same flow — you lose composition as soon as you hit a plain Future.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Future`** = blocking result handle; `.get()` waits, no callbacks, no composition.
- **`CompletableFuture`** implements `Future` + `CompletionStage`; full composable async API.
- CompletableFuture adds: callbacks, composition (`thenCompose`, `thenCombine`), exception recovery, manual completion, timeouts, executor control.
- `CompletableFuture` is a drop-in replacement for `Future` — it *is* a Future.
- **Default `supplyAsync` uses `commonPool`** — dangerous for blocking work; always pass an executor.
- **Java 21 virtual threads** often replace CompletableFuture chains for I/O-bound code; plain blocking `Future.get()` becomes viable again.
- CompletableFuture still wins for: callback wrapping, fan-out combinators, complex pipelines with recovery.
- **Never leave a CompletableFuture chain without a terminator** — exceptions vanish silently.
- For reactive streaming with backpressure, use Reactor/RxJava, not CompletableFuture.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`Future` is a **blocking result handle**; `CompletableFuture` is a **composable async pipeline**.

**Plain `Future<T>`**
- You get it from `ExecutorService.submit()`
- Can call `isDone()`, `cancel()`, or **`get()` which blocks**
- No callbacks, no composition, no exception handling
- Cannot be completed manually
- Fine for: single-task submit-and-block patterns

**`CompletableFuture<T>`**
- Implements `Future` — so it's a drop-in replacement
- Plus a full composable API:
  - Callbacks: `thenApply`, `thenAccept`, `thenRun`
  - Composition: `thenCompose` (sequential), `thenCombine` (parallel), `allOf`/`anyOf` (fan-in)
  - Exception handling: `exceptionally`, `handle`, `whenComplete`
  - Manual completion: `.complete(value)`, `.completeExceptionally(ex)`
  - Timeouts (Java 9+): `orTimeout`, `completeOnTimeout`
  - Executor control: `*Async(fn, executor)` variants

**The `supplyAsync` trap**
- `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task)` without an executor uses `ForkJoinPool.commonPool`
- Sized for CPU work (cores - 1)
- Blocking I/O on commonPool saturates it; all parallel streams stall
- **Always pass an executor for blocking work**

**Java 21 shifts the balance**
- Virtual threads make blocking `Future.get()` cheap again
- Simple blocking code on a virtual thread executor often reads better than CompletableFuture chains
- CompletableFuture remains essential for:
  - Wrapping callback-based libraries
  - Parallel fan-out with combinators (`allOf(f1, ..., fN)`)
  - Complex pipelines with multi-stage exception recovery

**When to use plain Future**
- Working with a legacy API that returns Future
- Simple submit-and-block patterns
- Java 21 + virtual threads, where blocking is cheap and composition is overkill

**When to use CompletableFuture**
- Non-trivial async flows with composition/timeout/recovery
- Wrapping callback-based libraries
- Public API you want callers to chain onto

**When neither is the right tool**
- Backpressured streaming → Reactor `Flux`/RxJava `Observable`
- Pure CPU work → parallel streams or `ForkJoinPool`

**Recommendation:** On **Java 8–17**, default to **`CompletableFuture` for any async flow with more than one stage**; the composition API saves you from callback hell and manual blocking. Always **pass a custom executor** to `*Async` methods for blocking work. On **Java 21+**, re-evaluate: for I/O-bound request handlers, **virtual threads with plain blocking `Future.get()`** often wins on readability. Reserve CompletableFuture for **true parallel fan-out** (`allOf` over many calls) and **callback wrapping**. Always **terminate chains** with `exceptionally` or `handle` — unterminated chains silently eat exceptions and produce the nastiest kind of production bug.

questions.question: What's the difference between `volatile` and `synchronized`? When is `volatile` enough?
questions.title: `volatile` vs `synchronized` — Visibility vs Atomicity
questions.direct_answer: **`volatile`** gives you only **visibility** — writes are immediately visible to all threads, and reads/writes can't be reordered across the `volatile` access. It does **NOT** give atomicity of compound operations. **`synchronized`** gives you both **mutual exclusion** (only one thread in the block at a time) and **visibility** (happens-before on lock acquire/release). **`volatile` is enough** for: flags (`volatile boolean running`), DCL's instance reference, single-writer-multi-reader scalars, and publishing references to immutable objects. **`volatile` is NOT enough** for compound operations like increment (`counter++` is read-modify-write, three operations), check-then-act (`if (!cache.contains(k)) cache.put(k,v)`), or any state involving multiple fields. For those, use `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, or an `Atomic*` class (which uses CAS internally). The biggest trap: making a counter `volatile` and thinking `counter++` is now thread-safe. It's not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the JMM distinction between visibility (volatile) and atomicity (synchronized), and can identify compound operations where volatile is insufficient
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming `volatile counter++` is atomic — it isn't. Thinking synchronized doesn't provide visibility (it does). Using volatile for multi-field state
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cite specific use cases where volatile is enough (flags, DCL, immutable publication) vs not enough (counter, compound check-then-act). Mention that on Java 21, ReentrantLock is often preferable to synchronized due to virtual-thread pinning

sections.title: Two Different Guarantees
sections.content:
Java concurrency has two distinct concerns:

- **Visibility** — when one thread writes a value, when does another thread see it? Without any memory-model guarantee, a write could sit in a CPU cache indefinitely, invisible to other cores.
- **Atomicity** — is a compound operation (read-then-write, or multiple writes) indivisible from another thread's perspective?

**`volatile`** provides **visibility and ordering** but NOT compound atomicity.
- Writes to a `volatile` field are flushed; reads are not cached.
- Establishes happens-before: everything before a volatile write is visible after a volatile read of the same field.
- But `x++` is read → modify → write, and another thread can interleave between steps.

**`synchronized`** provides **mutual exclusion + visibility**.
- Only one thread in the critical section at a time.
- Lock acquire/release establishes happens-before, giving the same visibility as volatile.
- Compound operations are safe because no other thread can interleave.

Knowing which is which saves you from a class of bugs that only manifest under load.

sections.title: volatile vs synchronized
sections.content:
| Aspect | `volatile` | `synchronized` |
|---|---|---|
| **Visibility guarantee** | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Prevents reordering** | ✅ (around the volatile access) | ✅ (around the block) |
| **Mutual exclusion** | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Compound atomicity** (e.g., `x++`) | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Multi-field consistency** | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Overhead** | Low (memory barrier on read/write) | Higher (monitor lock) |
| **Performance on contended reads** | Fast | Slower |
| **Deadlock risk** | None | Yes |
| **Pinning on virtual threads (Java 21)** | No | Yes — use `ReentrantLock` to avoid |
| **Can block** | No | Yes (waiting for lock) |
| **Typical use** | Flags, DCL, immutable publication | Critical sections, compound state |

sections.title: When `volatile` is Enough — Flag, DCL, Publication
When `volatile` is NOT Enough — The Classic Bugs
Performance and When to Choose
sections.content:
**`volatile` cost**:
- Compile to memory-barrier instructions on x86/ARM — usually a few nanoseconds.
- Read cost is very low; write cost is slightly higher due to cache flush.
- No blocking — always makes progress.

**`synchronized` cost**:
- Uncontended: JVM biased locking optimizes to near-volatile cost.
- Contended: blocking threads, context switches, monitor queue management — 100x worse than volatile.
- Under extreme contention: use `ReentrantLock` (tryLock, timeouts, fairness options).

**Rule of thumb**: if you only need visibility of a single scalar, prefer `volatile`. If you need atomicity or involve multiple fields, use `synchronized` or atomics. If you need advanced features (tryLock, fairness, Condition variables), use `ReentrantLock`.

**Java 21 caveat**: `synchronized` blocks containing blocking I/O **pin virtual threads** to their carrier. For new code targeting virtual threads, prefer `ReentrantLock`, which doesn't pin. `volatile` doesn't pin.

sections.title: Decision Guide
sections.content:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Stop flag, heartbeat, simple scalar published once per write | **`volatile`** |
| Double-checked locking instance reference | **`volatile`** (required) |
| Publish immutable object | **`volatile` reference** |
| Counter (increment / decrement) | **`AtomicInteger`** or **`LongAdder`** |
| Compound check-then-act | **`synchronized`** or **`ReentrantLock`** or **`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent`** |
| Multi-field consistent update | **`synchronized`** + encapsulation, or immutable object + volatile ref swap |
| Coordinate threads (wait/notify, signals) | **`synchronized` + wait/notify**, or **`ReentrantLock` + `Condition`** |
| Java 21+ with blocking I/O in lock | **`ReentrantLock`** (avoids pinning) |

**Watch out for**:
- **Compound ops on volatile** — the classic bug; always atomic/synchronized.
- **Volatile array/map** — the reference is volatile but the contents aren't thread-safe unless the collection is.
- **Over-synchronizing** — if you only need visibility of one scalar, don't lock.
- **Under-synchronizing** — "my reads are `volatile`, should be fine" — watch for multi-field invariants.
- **`synchronized` pinning on Java 21** — migrate to `ReentrantLock` for hot-path I/O.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`volatile`** — visibility + ordering only; compound operations NOT atomic.
- **`synchronized`** — mutual exclusion + visibility; compound operations safe.
- **`volatile` is enough** for: flags, DCL reference, immutable publication, single-value scalars.
- **`volatile` is NOT enough** for: counters (`x++`), check-then-act, multi-field invariants.
- For atomic compound numeric ops, use **`AtomicInteger`/`AtomicLong`** (or `LongAdder` for high contention).
- **`synchronized` has higher overhead** under contention; `volatile` is always non-blocking.
- **Java 21 pinning**: `synchronized` pins virtual threads; `ReentrantLock` doesn't, `volatile` doesn't.
- **Don't volatile a mutable collection reference** and expect thread safety — the collection contents aren't protected.
- **Writing code that looks right but isn't** is the #1 volatile failure mode — always trace the compound operation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`volatile` and `synchronized` solve overlapping but distinct problems in the Java Memory Model.

**`volatile` — visibility and ordering**
- Writes are flushed immediately; reads don't cache
- Establishes happens-before: writes before a volatile write are visible after the matching read
- Prevents reordering around the volatile access
- **Does NOT provide atomicity** for compound operations
- Non-blocking, very low overhead

**`synchronized` — mutual exclusion + visibility**
- Only one thread in the block at a time
- Lock acquire/release gives the same visibility as volatile
- Compound operations are safe because no interleaving
- Higher overhead under contention
- Can deadlock
- **Pins virtual threads on Java 21** — use `ReentrantLock` instead for hot-path I/O

**When `volatile` is enough**
- Single-scalar flag: `volatile boolean running` — one writer, many readers
- Double-checked locking instance reference
- Publishing an immutable object reference: `volatile Config config; config = newConfig;`
- Last-write-wins scalars: timestamps, sequence numbers

**When `volatile` is NOT enough**

**The canonical bug — counter increment**:
- `volatile int counter; counter++;`
- `counter++` is read → add → write, three separate operations
- Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6; you lose an increment
- Fix: `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`, or `LongAdder` for high contention, or `synchronized`

**Check-then-act**:
- `if (!cache.containsKey(k)) cache.put(k, v);`
- Two threads both see missing, both insert; one wins, logic inconsistent
- Fix: `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent`

**Multi-field consistency**:
- `volatile int x, y; x = 1; y = 2;`
- Another thread can see x updated but y not yet
- Fix: synchronized block, or encapsulate `(x,y)` in immutable object + volatile reference

**Performance**
- `volatile`: always a few nanoseconds, never blocks
- `synchronized`: uncontended is cheap (JVM biased locking); contended is 100x worse
- `ReentrantLock`: similar cost, more features (tryLock, fairness, Condition)

**Decision guide**
- Flag / single scalar / immutable ref → `volatile`
- Counter / arithmetic atomicity → `AtomicInteger` / `LongAdder`
- Compound state / check-then-act → `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`
- Virtual threads with blocking I/O in lock → `ReentrantLock`

**Recommendation:** Default to **`volatile`** when you have a single scalar and just need visibility — it's the cheapest and non-blocking. Use **atomic classes** (`AtomicInteger`, `AtomicReference`) for compound numeric operations; they give lock-free CAS-based atomicity. Use **`synchronized`** or **`ReentrantLock`** when you need mutual exclusion across multiple fields or complex state. **On Java 21+**, prefer `ReentrantLock` over `synchronized` for any hot path that performs blocking I/O, because `synchronized` pins virtual threads and starves carriers. The cardinal rule: whenever you find yourself thinking "this is just a counter, I'll make it volatile," stop — that's the #1 source of production bugs in this area.

questions.question: Virtual threads vs platform threads in Java 21 — full comparison of footprint, cost, scheduling, and compatibility.
questions.title: Virtual Threads vs Platform Threads in Java 21 — Complete Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **Platform threads** are traditional `java.lang.Thread` instances backed 1:1 by **OS kernel threads** — ~1 MB stack, ~1 ms creation, scheduled preemptively by the OS, limited to ~thousands per JVM. **Virtual threads** (Java 21 JEP 444) are lightweight JVM-managed threads scheduled onto a small pool of **carrier** platform threads. Stack is resizable (stored on the heap, KB not MB), creation is microseconds, and you can have **millions** concurrently. Both are subclasses of `java.lang.Thread` and expose the same API, so existing code just works. The tradeoffs: virtual threads **pin** on `synchronized` blocks and native frames (JVM can't unmount them), which under load can starve carriers. They don't add CPU parallelism — parallelism is still capped at CPU count. **Use virtual threads** for I/O-bound server code (REST APIs, message handlers, HTTP fan-out). **Use platform threads** for CPU-bound pools (`ForkJoinPool`) and when working with legacy `synchronized`-heavy code you can't refactor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the fundamental differences (OS-backed vs JVM-scheduled, memory footprint, blocking behavior) and can pick the right type for a given workload
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming virtual threads always beat platform threads. Not recognizing that CPU-bound work doesn't benefit. Forgetting about pinning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention concrete numbers (1MB vs KB, thousands vs millions), the mount/unmount scheduling model, pinning on synchronized, and that `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` on Spring Boot 3.2+ is a one-line migration for request handlers

sections.title: The Core Difference
sections.content:
**Platform threads** (classic Java threads) are 1:1-mapped to OS kernel threads. Every `new Thread()` causes a syscall to create a native thread. The OS scheduler manages them preemptively; stack sizes are fixed (default 1 MB on most JVMs); memory per thread is ~1 MB + kernel bookkeeping. You can create ~5–10K before running out of memory or hitting OS limits.

**Virtual threads** (Java 21 GA) are **scheduled by the JVM** onto a small pool of **carrier platform threads** (by default, a `ForkJoinPool` sized to CPU count). They're still `java.lang.Thread` subclasses — same API — but stacks are stored on the heap as resizable objects, starting at a few KB. Creation is pure-Java and takes microseconds. You can have **millions** concurrent.

The big idea: when a virtual thread hits blocking I/O, the JVM **unmounts** it from the carrier — stack goes to the heap, carrier goes to another virtual thread. When I/O completes, the virtual thread is rescheduled onto any free carrier. The result: thread-per-request server code that scales to millions of concurrent I/O-bound requests without async/reactive complexity.

Both thread types coexist. Virtual threads *are* a kind of Thread; `Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()` tells them apart.

sections.title: Full Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Dimension | Platform Thread | Virtual Thread |
|---|---|---|
| **Backed by** | OS kernel thread (1:1) | JVM schedules onto carrier |
| **Carrier** | Self (it IS the OS thread) | `ForkJoinPool` of platform threads (= CPU count) |
| **Stack size** | Fixed, ~1 MB default | Resizable, starts KB, on heap |
| **Creation cost** | ~1 ms (syscall) | ~microseconds (pure Java) |
| **Memory per thread** | ~1 MB + kernel | ~few KB (varies with stack depth) |
| **Max practical** | Thousands (5K-10K) | **Millions** (limited by heap) |
| **Scheduling** | Preemptive by OS | Cooperative by JVM at blocking points |
| **Blocking I/O behavior** | OS parks the thread | JVM unmounts; carrier serves others |
| **CPU parallelism** | Thread count | Carrier count (= CPU count) |
| **Concurrency ceiling** | Memory and OS limits | Heap only |
| **`Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()`** | `false` | `true` |
| **ThreadLocal** | Normal overhead | Works but expensive at scale — prefer `ScopedValue` |
| **`synchronized` block** | Normal | **Pins** the carrier — can starve under load |
| **Native (JNI) frames** | Normal | **Pin** — can't unmount while present |
| **Creation API** | `new Thread()`, `Executors.new*ThreadPool` | `Thread.ofVirtual().start()`, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` |
| **Pooling** | Yes — essential for cost amortization | **No** — create one per task, they're cheap |
| **Best for** | CPU-bound work, legacy code | I/O-bound, high-concurrency server code |
| **Not suited for** | Massive concurrency (too heavy) | Pure CPU computation, `synchronized`-heavy code |

sections.title: Creating Each Type
The Scheduling Model — Mount and Unmount
sections.content:
The JVM maintains a **scheduler** (a `ForkJoinPool` by default, parallelism = CPU count) of carrier platform threads. Virtual threads are queued on this scheduler.

**When a virtual thread runs**:
1. Scheduler picks an idle carrier.
2. Virtual thread's continuation (captured stack) is restored onto the carrier.
3. Task executes.

**When the virtual thread hits blocking I/O** (`Socket.read`, `HttpClient.send`, JDBC, etc.):
1. The JDK's instrumented blocking call triggers `Continuation.yield()`.
2. The virtual thread's stack is copied to the heap.
3. Carrier is released back to the scheduler.
4. Scheduler picks up another waiting virtual thread.

**When I/O completes**:
1. Kernel notification (via `epoll`/`kqueue`) wakes the virtual thread.
2. Scheduler picks a free carrier.
3. Continuation is restored; execution resumes at the blocking point.

**Platform threads don't do this dance** — they just block, and the OS parks them. Memory stays pinned; the kernel manages context switches.

**Parallelism**: on both models, only `#carriers` (or `#platform-threads`) can actually execute at once. What changes is **concurrency** — how many tasks can be in-flight. Virtual threads let concurrency approach millions without running out of threads.

sections.title: Key Gotchas — Pinning and ThreadLocal
sections.content:
**Pinning on `synchronized`**:
A virtual thread inside a `synchronized` block **cannot unmount**. Blocking I/O inside the block holds the carrier. Under load, many pinned virtual threads = all carriers busy waiting on I/O = **carrier exhaustion**. System appears frozen; CPU at 0%.

**Fix**: migrate `synchronized` wrapping blocking I/O to `ReentrantLock`, which uses Loom-aware `LockSupport.park()`.

Detect pinning:
```bash
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full MyApp
# or in production via JFR: jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event
```

**Pinning on native (JNI) frames**:
While JNI is on the stack, the JVM can't capture the continuation — virtual thread pins. Usually fine unless your hot path does heavy native work.

**ThreadLocal at scale**:
Each virtual thread carries its own copies of ThreadLocals. A million virtual threads × large ThreadLocal state = heap exhaustion. Options:
- Remove per-thread caches (they're anti-patterns anyway).
- Keep small ThreadLocals (MDC for logging is fine).
- For immutable per-scope values, migrate to **`ScopedValue`** (Java 21 preview, stable later).

**Downstream saturation**:
Your old 200-thread pool implicitly rate-limited DB calls. Virtual threads remove that limit; a million requests can hammer a 20-connection HikariCP pool. Add **`Semaphore`** or **Resilience4j Bulkhead** for explicit flow control.

sections.title: Which Type to Use When
sections.content:
**Use platform threads when**:
- **CPU-bound work** — image processing, heavy parsing, encryption, math. Virtual threads don't add CPU parallelism.
- Fixed pool sized to cores for compute (`ForkJoinPool`, `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores)`).
- Legacy code with heavy `synchronized` usage around I/O that's expensive to refactor.
- Library code using `ThreadLocal` for large per-thread caches that can't be easily refactored.
- Java version < 21.

**Use virtual threads when**:
- **I/O-bound server code** — REST APIs with DB + downstream HTTP calls.
- High concurrency (thousands of simultaneous connections).
- Outbound fan-out (make 1000 parallel HTTP calls).
- Message consumer dispatching each message to its own task.
- Existing code using `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` for blocking I/O — virtual threads often simplify.
- Thread-pool sizing headaches that come from unpredictable load patterns.

**Hybrid is common**:
- Virtual threads for request dispatch and I/O orchestration.
- Dedicated `ForkJoinPool` (platform threads) for CPU-heavy slices within a request.
- Offload via `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(cpuTask, cpuPool).join()` from the virtual thread.

**Watch out for**:
- **Pinning audit** — must be done before production migration.
- **Downstream flow control** — new concern once thread count no longer limits concurrency.
- **Observability** — thread dumps differ; `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file` for the new format.
- **Don't pool virtual threads** — defeats the purpose.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Platform threads** = 1:1 OS kernel threads; ~1 MB, slow to create, thousands max.
- **Virtual threads** = JVM-scheduled onto carrier pool; KB, fast to create, millions possible.
- Both are `java.lang.Thread` subclasses — same API.
- Virtual threads **unmount** on blocking I/O, freeing the carrier.
- **Parallelism unchanged** = CPU count; **concurrency** can scale to millions.
- **`synchronized` pins** virtual threads — migrate to `ReentrantLock` for I/O-heavy locks.
- **Don't pool virtual threads** — create one per task; they're cheap.
- **Spring Boot 3.2+**: `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` one-line migration for request handlers.
- **Virtual threads are for I/O concurrency**, not CPU parallelism.
- **Hybrid**: virtual threads for I/O + platform `ForkJoinPool` for CPU-heavy stages.
- **New operational concern**: downstream flow control via `Semaphore` (thread count no longer rate-limits).
- **Adoption caveat**: audit for `synchronized` + I/O pinning and heavy ThreadLocal usage first.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Platform threads and virtual threads differ fundamentally in how they're scheduled and what they cost.

**Platform threads — the classic**
- 1:1 mapped to OS kernel threads
- ~1 MB stack, created via syscall (~1 ms)
- Scheduled preemptively by the OS
- Memory per thread dominates — thousands is the practical ceiling
- Good for CPU-bound work (ForkJoinPool, fixed pool sized to cores)

**Virtual threads — Java 21 Project Loom**
- Scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier platform threads (by default, ForkJoinPool sized to CPU count)
- Stack stored on the heap as a resizable object — KB, not MB
- Creation is microseconds, pure Java
- Millions concurrent
- Subclass of `java.lang.Thread` — same API, existing code just works
- Can detect with `Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()`

**The mount/unmount mechanism**
- Virtual thread starts running on a carrier
- Hits blocking I/O — JDK's instrumented blocking call triggers `Continuation.yield()`
- Stack copied to heap; carrier freed to serve another virtual thread
- I/O completes — kernel notification wakes the virtual thread
- Scheduler picks any free carrier; continuation restored; execution resumes

**The killer numbers**
- Platform: ~1 MB → max ~5K-10K threads
- Virtual: ~few KB → **millions**
- Parallelism unchanged: still capped at CPU count
- Concurrency: limited by heap, not thread count

**Creating each**
- Platform: `new Thread()`, `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)`
- Virtual: `Thread.ofVirtual().start()`, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, `Thread.startVirtualThread()`
- Spring Boot 3.2+: `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`

**Don't pool virtual threads** — creation is free; one-per-task is the pattern

**The gotchas**

**Pinning on `synchronized`**:
- While inside `synchronized`, virtual thread can't unmount
- Blocking I/O inside synchronized holds a carrier
- Under load: carrier exhaustion; system appears frozen
- Fix: migrate to `ReentrantLock` (Loom-aware via `LockSupport.park`)
- Detect: `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` or JFR `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned`

**Pinning on native (JNI) frames**:
- Fundamental; native code can't participate in continuation mechanism
- Usually fine unless hot path does heavy native work

**ThreadLocal at scale**:
- Each virtual thread carries its own copy
- Millions of threads × large ThreadLocals = heap pressure
- Alternative: `ScopedValue` (Java 21 preview) for immutable per-scope values

**Downstream saturation**:
- Old 200-thread pool implicitly rate-limited DB connections
- Virtual threads remove that limit; must add explicit `Semaphore` or Bulkhead

**Decision guide**
- **CPU-bound work** → platform threads (ForkJoinPool)
- **I/O-bound server code** → virtual threads
- **Legacy synchronized-heavy** → platform threads or refactor first
- **Java < 21** → no choice, platform threads
- **Hybrid**: virtual for I/O, platform ForkJoinPool for CPU slices offloaded via CompletableFuture

**Recommendation:** On **Java 21+**, default to **virtual threads for server-side I/O-bound code** — `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or Spring Boot's `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`. Keep **platform threads for CPU-bound pools** (`ForkJoinPool.commonPool`, fixed platform-thread pools sized to cores). Before migrating existing code, **audit for `synchronized` around blocking I/O** (migrate to `ReentrantLock`) and **large ThreadLocal state** (reduce or move to `ScopedValue`), and **add explicit downstream flow control** via `Semaphore` because thread count no longer implicitly rate-limits you. Don't rewrite working Netty/WebFlux systems just because virtual threads exist — the migration cost exceeds the benefit; save them for new code and thread-per-request refactors.

groups.heading: Platform thread
groups.text: Maps 1:1 to an OS kernel thread. ~1MB stack. Thread creation triggers a syscall. Expensive — you need a pool to reuse them. Blocking one means blocking an OS thread.

groups.heading: Virtual thread
groups.text: JVM-managed, mounted on carrier threads. Heap-allocated stack — starts tiny, grows on demand. Blocking a virtual thread unmounts it from the carrier, freeing the OS thread for other work.

groups.heading: Virtual threads
groups.text: I/O-bound workloads with many concurrent connections — HTTP servers, database calls, file I/O. The thread-per-request model works again.

groups.heading: Platform threads
groups.text: CPU-bound work — virtual threads don't help. The gotcha: virtual threads can be pinned to a carrier by synchronized blocks and native code — avoid those in hot I/O paths.

beats.text: Tomcat with platform threads: 200 threads, 200 concurrent requests max before queuing. Same app with virtual threads: one virtual thread per request, no pool needed. 10,000 concurrent requests, each blocking on a DB call — virtual threads handle it, platform threads don't.

speakable_v2.cap: Virtual threads for I/O-bound work at scale. Platform threads for CPU-bound. Virtual threads shine when blocking is the bottleneck.
